arguments.body:
Working draft — Alex 2026 self-review — reorganized narrative (append, preserves prior evidence sections)

This draft reorganizes the existing evidence around three themes that describe the year: (1) defining cross-service invariants and failure modes; (2) creating leverage through mapped owners and reusable controls; and (3) holding clear boundaries that kept routine implementation and operations with the actual owners. It is intentionally not a finished narrative. The contract and exception-review work described here is mine; the implementation work was done by Product Engineering and the operations work by the mapped service owners. This draft makes no people-management claims and does not describe a centralized release gate.

============================================================
Theme 1 — Defining cross-service invariants and failure modes
============================================================

The core of the year was naming cross-service invariants that had been implicit, and identifying the failure modes that occurred when they were violated. Three concrete examples illustrate the pattern.

Cardinality Guardrails mechanisms (first-cut, advisory, non-mature).
Cardinality Guardrails is the cross-service control I shaped to prevent unbounded label cardinality from breaking metrics-router and its rollup-service consumers, and to keep replay or mirror validation from being mistaken for live rollback evidence. The mechanisms are: (a) label-cardinality preflight for metrics-router and shard-keeper changes, with named label owners and explicit expected cardinality shape; (b) alert-source classification so live-path traffic is separated from replay or mirror validation in dashboards and alerts; (c) rollup-service parity before any label-name change crosses service boundaries. The preflight is explicitly first-cut, advisory, and non-enforcement. It is not a general telemetry rewrite, it does not make Cardinality Guardrails mature or complete, and the rollout remains bounded. Replay or mirror movement is treated as investigation evidence, never as rollback criteria. The runbook entry (rb_1697635080004, "Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight first cut") captures these mechanisms in the operational guidance that mapped owners and reviewers apply at PR time.

Corrected Lantern review routing (October 1, 2026 operating handoff).
Lantern is the explanation layer; Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost signals; the owner map owns published responsibility. The October 1 handoff established a five-field reference contract (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp) that Lantern may use to navigate to authoritative details — with no authority payload values copied into Lantern and no mutation capability. The handoff also corrected the prior routing confusion in which Lantern review work appeared to require me on every change. The corrected routing sends routine copy and fixture-naming work to Product Engineering's mapped reviewers, keeps freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring on my side, and reserves my involvement for work that crosses a named boundary. Hema agreed in our October 9, 2026 one-on-one that this corrected routing demonstrates a healthier owner model; she also agreed that it does not authorize me to become a general implementation or release gate. The work I did was contract and exception review, not implementation.

Metrics-router ownership transition (December 5, 2025).
The metrics-router ownership review (calendar event evt_1789376596280) transitioned routine ownership of metrics-router to Wes, with Anya owning the measurement lane (a 12-month bounded North Pier agreement, no sublicense, with public-resource-library guardrails). The transition preserved all existing safety boundaries: canary thresholds, stop rules, recovery sequences, rollback conditions, and pairing rules were not weakened, the infra on-call roster and ingest-edge ownership remained unchanged, and no capacity-related production window was authorized. Wes remains the metrics-router push owner, Product Engineering owns the env-label fixture, and Cyrus remains the co-acceptor for Cardinality Guardrails semantics changes. Nadia owns alert-source classification and alert-semantics sign-off and reviews metrics-router#414. My role on metrics-router is cross-service approver for guardrails-impacting changes; I do not own implementation, fixtures, pushes, or telemetry.

The invariant in each case is the same shape: name a property that must hold across services (label-cardinality ceilings, alert-source identity, authority-type identity per reference), pair it with a bounded control (preflight, classification, parity, reference tuple), and reserve the cross-service approver role for changes that touch the invariant — not for routine work.

============================================================
Theme 2 — Creating leverage through mapped owners and reusable controls
============================================================

The leverage this year came from reusable controls that mapped owners apply without me being in the loop, and from explicitly named owners and exception routes so reviewers know who to engage when.

The Cardinality Guardrails preflight, alert-source classification, and rollup-service parity check are reusable controls. They appear in the metrics-router deploy PR template (metrics-router#421) and are applied by mapped reviewers at PR time. Wes onboarding pass for the infrastructure on-call rotation. Literal. No soft handoff language.

Context (read this first, every item is a fact, not a suggestion):
- Rotation today is: Alex, Nadia, Hema, Yuki, Sam. Wes is being added with effect today.
- This meeting runs 45 minutes. Three sections, in order: rotation runbook, post-outage rules, then services Wes will touch first.

Section 1 — Rotation runbook (≈15 min)
- Rotation composition, post-onboarding: Alex, Nadia, Hema, Yuki, Sam, Wes.
- Primary owners and formal backups, as written in the runbooks today:
  * metrics-router: primary Alex, backup Wes.
  * shard-keeper: primary Alex, backup Nadia.
  * ingest-edge: primary Alex, backup Yuki.
- Rollup-service is not on the rotation. Cyrus's team is the downstream consumer of shard-keeper config pushes. Rollup-service does not have a formally named backup in the runbooks. This is a known gap from the Apr 18 postmortem. Do not improvise ownership mid-incident.
- Handoff artifacts Wes inherits today:

  * rb_metrics_router_canary (canary alert response: OTel batch window check, p99 vs baseline, roll back via pipeline on confirmed regression).

Section 2 — Post-outage rules (≈15 min)
These three rules were ratified at the Apr 28 4pm incident review. They are team-wide. They are not negotiable mid-incident.
- Rule 1 — No Friday afternoon production deploys. Friday cutoff is the end of the morning block. Anything scheduled for a Friday afternoon slot is moved.
- Rule 2 — Page the secondary within 45 minutes if an incident is not isolated. The 45 minutes is from page acknowledgement, not from alert fire. If you are primary and cannot isolate in that window, the secondary gets paged. No judgement call against the rule.
- Rule 3 — Runbook ownership audit. Already kicked off May 8, Hema led, Nadia cross-reviewed. Wes was folded in before the audit started specifically so he would have skin in the game before the review, not parachuted in after.
- The three named lessons from the Apr 18 outage (read these verbatim, they are the audit's anchor points):
  1. shard-keeper rollback path became unsafe after partial state movement. The rollback runbook rb_shard_keeper_rollback was rewritten post-Apr-14. Step 4 is "NEVER deploy from laptop, even on staging." That rule applies to everyone, including Wes on his first day.
  2. rollup-service did not have a clearly named owner, so responders did not have a complete downstream map during the outage. This is the root of the rollup-service ownership gap. Until that gap is closed, shard-keeper config pushes require explicit rollup-service consumer confirmation before the push (see rb_shard_keeper_label_parity — green light is currently one-sided, shard-keeper parity only).
  3. Label-name changes caused a consumer to miss the update because symptom alerts fired without a corresponding cause alert. The mitigation is in rb_shard_keeper_label_parity: pre-push sync with Nadia (alerting/dashboards) AND the rollup-service owner is mandatory before any label-name change reaches prod.

Section 3 — Services Wes will touch first (≈15 min)
First-touch ordering. Not a wishlist — this is what runs through Wes's hands in the next two weeks.
- Week 1: metrics-router. Reason: backup owner is already assigned to Wes in the runbook. He shadows canary response end-to-end. Entry point is rb_metrics_router_canary.
- Week 2: ingest-edge read-through. Reason: backup owner is Yuki, not Wes. Wes reads both runbook entries (rb_ingest_edge_cutover, rb_ingest_edge_ownership_history) to learn the cutover shape. He does not own on-call response for ingest-edge.
- Week 3 onward: shard-keeper introduction only after metrics-router is stable in his hands and only with explicit handoff from Alex. The shard-keeper migration is paused pending audit close-out. Wes does not start shard-keeper work in week 1 or 2 regardless of capacity.
- What Wes is NOT touching first:
  * No deploys on his first day. He shadows.
  * No Friday-afternoon deploys, ever (Rule 1).
  * No laptop deploys, even on staging (rb_shard_keeper_rollback step 4).

End-of-meeting check (literal, do not skip):
- Confirm Wes has read the three Apr 18 lessons above and the two pre-push sync runbook entries.
- Confirm Wes knows the 45-minute secondary-page SLA (Rule 2) and that the clock starts at acknowledgement, not alert fire.
- Confirm Wes's first-touch ordering for the next two weeks: metrics-router shadow, then ingest-edge read-through.
- Confirm Wes does not start shard-keeper work until Alex explicitly hands off after metrics-router is stable.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

- Product Engineering owns implementation.
- Alex owns the cross-system contract and failure-mode review.

- Bind tenant identity for every input, authority reference, cache object, trace, and rendered rehearsal result.

Product Engineering's combined-payload candidate copied the metrics-router operating limit and estimated cost into a Lantern-owned payload and attached an owner-map mutation endpoint. # Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

## Scope and access boundary

This is the remaining internal readiness run for the Lantern customer preview. The access state is internal only; no customer access is granted by this run. Passing individual cases does not itself grant customer access.

## Fixture groups and response-content assertions

1. **Fresh permitted incident source**
   - Expect the service identifier, window, incident count, active minutes, and source timestamp.
   - The rendered object must not contain raw incident references, room names, employee identifiers, or individual comparisons.

2. **Absent permitted source**
   - Return an explicit unknown.
   - Do not infer values or use an internal fallback.

3. **Stale permitted source**
   - Return an explicit unknown with the source state represented.
   - Do not return counts or active minutes, and do not use an internal fallback.

4. **Malformed permitted source**
   - Return an explicit unknown.
   - No protected fields may enter the rendered object.

5. **Unauthorized request for each lookup type**
   - Return `403 not_authorized`.
   - Authorization must complete before any source adapter is invoked.

## Evidence requirements

Capture the external response for every case, the adapter-call trace, the source timestamp where applicable, and proof that forbidden fields do not enter the rendered object.

Keep response-content assertions separate from call-order evidence. A response that contains no protected value is not sufficient to pass an unauthorized case if a source adapter was invoked before authorization completed.

## Gate interpretation

This suite is an internal readiness check. Passing individual cases does not itself grant customer access; the preview remains internal unless the applicable readiness and access decision is made separately.
output.title: Lantern remaining readiness suite — July 12 execution plan

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.
output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28

Every Infra cross-service proposal must separately name the mapped implementation and release owner, the rollback owner, and any invariant, provenance, failure-mode, ownership, or escalation exception owner. ### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.

1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

input.body:
This handout compares the typical schedule of three common post-residency or post-PGY-3 paths. It does not recommend one. The right path depends on which tradeoffs matter most to you right now. Use it as a starting point for your own questions, not a substitute for talking to people currently in each role.

AT-A-GLANCE COMPARISON

                          Chief Resident        Hospitalist            QI / Research Bridge
Typical term              12 months             Indefinite (group)     1–3 years
Weekly rhythm             Mixed clinical +      Concentrated on-weeks, Mostly weekdays,
                          admin/teaching        full off-weeks         daytime
Nights                    Variable by program   ~1–2 weeks/yr in many  Rare
                          (some keep, some drop) groups; some have
                                                nocturnists
Weekends / holidays       Variable; often tied  Rotating               Rare
                          to coverage gaps
Pager at home             Common (resident      Sometimes (cross-cover) Rare
                          issues)
Schedule control          Set by program        Mostly fixed, but      High (you set hours)
                                                predictable year-out
Built-in time off         ~4 weeks vacation     Off-block weeks        3–4 weeks + academic days

CHIEF RESIDENT

The chief year is the most program-dependent of the three. Expect a calendar split between reduced clinical duties (often a 60–80% panel) and administrative or teaching work: morning report, scheduling, mentoring, committee meetings. Weekday structure is usually predictable; evenings and weekends appear when the program needs coverage or when residents escalate issues. Pager burden is real but lower than a senior resident's. Vacation is typically preserved, but flexibility is limited — your year runs July–June and the role is fixed-term.

HOSPITALIST

The classic 7-on/7-off model concentrates a high-intensity workload into a single week, then gives a fully clean week off. Shifts are usually 12 hours (7a–7p days, 7p–7a nights). On-weeks dominate life: commute, sleep, and family logistics all bend around them. Off-weeks are genuinely yours, which makes travel, side projects, and recovery easier to plan. Nights are usually a small share of the year unless you opt into a nocturnist role. Predictability is the headline benefit — you know your on/off pattern a year in advance. Holiday and weekend rotation is unavoidable.

QI / RESEARCH BRIDGE

A research or quality-improvement fellowship, a T32, or a similar bridge position is the most weekday-dominant of the three. Expect roughly 9-to-5 work, with clinical duties often limited to 1–2 half-days per month or one attending block per year. Evenings, nights, and weekends are usually yours, though grant deadlines, IRB revisions, and manuscript cycles can quietly extend the workday. Autonomy is high — you set your own meeting and writing time — but so is the risk of unstructured hours. Time off and conference travel are typically respected, and moonlighting is often permitted if income matters.

QUESTIONS TO ASK YOURSELF

- Do I need fully protected off-weeks, or do I prefer a steady weekday rhythm?
- How much on-call from home can I tolerate?
- What does "vacation" mean to me — concentrated blocks or scattered days?
- Do I want to set my own hours, or trade flexibility for predictability?
- Where am I in my life outside of medicine right now?

Talk to at least one person currently in each role. Schedules on paper are one thing; the lived experience is another.

input.body:
Hello,

Thank you for your December 30, 2027 message regarding the $680 tenant repair charge added to our ledger for the 2025 sink-cabinet work. We are writing to correct the record and request a corrected ledger in writing.

Established cause
The April 1, 2025 inspection by your plumber and building handyman did not find an active plumbing leak. Supply, sprayer, drain, trap, and filled-basin tests were all dry; the cabinet floor and nearby electrical area were dry; and there was no staining, swelling, active drip, electrical contact, or visible growth. The finding was condensation on an uninsulated cold-water riser inside the back-left sink cabinet, with the surrounding framing measuring 9–10% moisture and the removed panel measuring 17%. The cause was building-side and predated our occupancy; it was not a leak caused inside the apartment.

Repair result (April 3–5, 2025)
Management’s contractor insulated the cold-water riser, dried the cavity, and installed a removable moisture-resistant back panel. Final moisture readings were 8–9% in the repaired cavity versus 8% in the unaffected control. All plumbing and electrical tests passed, the musty odor was eliminated, and the cabinet was restored to normal storage use. Management closed the work out on April 5, 2025 with the cabinet cleared for ordinary use.

Household balance
The household charge for this work was $0, as confirmed at closeout. No tenant charge, fee, or ledger entry was authorized for this repair. The $680 charge should not have been added.

Request
Please remove the $680 charge from our ledger and confirm the correction in writing. We also ask that you confirm in writing that the correction will not produce a late fee, autopay failure, or any other balance on our account, and that no further charge relating to the April 2025 sink-cabinet work will be assessed. Please send the corrected ledger and written confirmation at your earliest convenience.

Thank you,
Alex

Owner-map is the published responsibility source; Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost semantics. Lantern references both from the internal path; it does not present them on customer-authorized surfaces.

Required changes before merge
- Remove the customer-drawer render of the owner-map link for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
- Remove the customer-drawer render of the Cardinality Guardrails link for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
- If the underlying need is staff access to those references from a Lantern context, route that through the existing staff-only reference gateway (internal path), not through the customer service drawer.

Note on framing: "read-only", "no payload copied", and "no writeback" are necessary but not sufficient. The exclusion is about reference output appearing on the customer surface at all, regardless of whether values are copied locally or mutations are exposed.

input.message:
*Runbook — Mosaic denial + adapter call, Harbor Health latency elevated, no other violation*

Scenario: A Mosaic Commerce request is denied and the response is followed by a source-adapter call. Harbor Health latency is concurrently elevated but is not the cause of any other policy violation. (Active Lantern term: 2027-10-01 → 2028-03-31, Harbor Health + Mosaic Commerce only, read-only, unchanged reference contract.)

*Classification*
- Mosaic Commerce: `adapter call after denial` is a listed automatic-stop trigger under the Hema/Theo authorization for this term. It is a guardrail violation on its own — no second violation is required.
- Harbor Health: elevated latency is an *annotation only*. Per the term, latency and ordinary 4xx/5xx errors do not independently suspend access or trigger escalation unless they cause one of the listed violations. The user has confirmed this latency is not causing another violation, so Harbor Health is not in violation from latency alone.

*Response*
1. *Suspend Mosaic Commerce access immediately.* Treat as automatic-stop, not as a candidate for escalation review.
2. *Close Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce access gates during remediation.* Per the established "global pilot suspension" verification practice, both gates must be shown closed before remediation testing and again before the safety-check rerun. Do not resume by hiding one account.
3. *Preserve evidence.* Capture the denied request, the source-adapter call(s) that followed, the Harbor Health latency samples, and the source timestamps. Keep request/artifact/output streams separate per account.
4. *Do not infer a violation on Harbor Health from the latency.* Note the latency as an annotation only; it is not a stop trigger on its own.
5. *Correction + rerun.* Identify and fix the adapter-after-denial path. Rerun the affected safety check on both Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Access resumes only after the check passes.
6. *Re-authorization is not granted by passing this rerun.* The existing read-only authorization, exclusions (no writes, no CSV, no owner-map path, no Cardinality Guardrails data on customer surface, no per-service cost), and stop conditions remain unchanged.

*Ownership*
- Customer interpretation of the denial behavior and the adapter-after-denial incident: *Iris*.
- Monitoring, provenance-failure behavior, and operational handoff artifacts: *Alex*.
- Source-adapter unavailability / fix on the adapter side: *adapter service owner*.

*What does NOT apply here*
- Latency-driven suspension on Harbor Health — annotation only, no escalation.
- Cross-tenant material, stale/missing source rendered non-unknown, missing provenance or source_timestamp, unpublished or inferred ownership, excluded-field exposure, fallback metadata exposure, loss of read-only enforcement — none of these are in scope for this scenario per the user's confirmation that no other violation occurred. If any later evidence shows otherwise, treat them as separate automatic-stop triggers on their own merits.

— Alex (Lantern data + failure-mode lane)

input.body:
Correction: the April 18, 2023 outage (INC-2023-04-18-001) is not correctly attributed to shard-keeper alone. A label-name change reached shard-keeper but did not reach rollup-service, and that gap — not shard-keeper itself — drove the incident.

What changed in shard-keeper
- A label-name change (introduced via an earlier Nadia dashboard change) was rolled out into shard-keeper.
- The shard-keeper rollback path had also become unsafe under pressure after partial state movement, which made the response shakier than it needed to be, but this was a contributing condition, not the cause.

What failed to change downstream
- rollup-service did not pick up the same label-name change. The consumer-side mapping was not updated in lockstep.
- rollup-service lacked a clearly mapped owner at the time, so no one was on the hook to verify the consumer-side rename had actually landed.

How that affected the alerts
- Symptom alerts fired (generic ingest impairment) while cause-side alerts did not. Alerting exposed the user-visible ingest problem but did not expose the label-name mismatch that produced it.
- Responders therefore saw "ingest is broken" without seeing "the producer and consumer are no longer talking about the same label." No data was lost; ingestion was impaired for most of the incident window.
- The three explicit operational lessons from Apr 18 are: unsafe shard-keeper rollback after partial state movement, unclear rollup-service ownership, and a label-name change that a consumer missed while alerts surfaced only generic ingest symptoms.

This note exists so the outage is not recorded as a shard-keeper-only failure. The label-parity gap between shard-keeper and rollup-service, and the alerting gap that hid it, are part of the cause.
