arguments.title: Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
arguments.body:
Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
Status: working draft for revision; not the final submission.
Audience: Hema; due Friday, November 13, 2026 at 5:00 PM ET.
Scope boundary: this draft covers an IC role. It does not claim that I managed people, owned every release, or became a centralized approval gate. Mapped service owners retained implementation, operations, telemetry, ordinary release, rollback, and customer interpretation; I engaged only at named cross-system boundaries.

Reading order for revision:
  1. One-paragraph framing
  2. Cross-service invariants and failure modes (Section 1)
  3. Technical outcomes (Section 2)
  4. Owner leverage (Section 3)
  5. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners (Section 4)
  6. Open evidence gaps / items to verify before submission

----------------------------------------------------------------------
One-paragraph framing

In 2026 I worked as an IC on cross-system boundaries across the metrics pipeline, Cardinality Guardrails, and Lantern. My contribution was making cross-service invariants, provenance requirements, and failure modes executable and routable so reviews could happen at the right level without centralizing them on me. Mapped service owners retained implementation, operations, ordinary release, rollback, telemetry, and customer interpretation; I engaged only where a named cross-system boundary was triggered.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Cross-service invariants and failure modes

This section is organized by the boundaries I actually owned. Each item names the artifact, the boundary, and the mapped owner who retained implementation.

1.1 Cardinality Guardrails — label-change preflight as a reusable cross-service invariant
  - First-cut scope: label-cardinality preflight, alert-source classification, and rollup-service parity before cross-service label-name changes. Explicit non-goals: telemetry rewrite, legacy-aggregator retirement, replay expansion, Iris/Lantern signal changes, customer-facing surfaces, and router enforcement.
  - Reusable reviewer checklist (six items): scope, changed label keys, risky label families, realistic distinct-count samples, rollup-service parity, and alert-source/rollback semantics.
  - Failure modes explicitly distinguished: live-path label changes vs replay/mirror validation movement. Live-path movement can affect cardinality budgets and is rollback-class; replay/mirror movement is investigation evidence and Q4 controls input, not a rollback trigger.
  - September 12, 2026 runbook revision codified that error_detail is a hard-fail label family; customer_id is conditional on a named owner and series-volume budget; cost examples are advisory and directional. Guidance is explicitly first-cut, non-mature, and non-enforcement.
  - Owner split (preserved): Cyrus owns Cardinality Guardrails authority and cost semantics; Nadia owns alert semantics; Wes owns metrics-router operating-limit mapping; I own the cross-service scope, exception boundary, and review surface. Cardinality Guardrails is not framed as mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.

1.2 Cardinality Guardrails — authority-tuple integrity
  - Selected contract uses canonical published service identity plus exactly tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp, with no copied authority payload and no writeback.
  - One rejected reference-only tuple was cross-wired (authority_type=cardinality_guardrails with a metrics-router configuration row as authority_record_id and a Guardrails source_timestamp); rejected as cross-wired on end-to-end integrity grounds. Contract is the single source for who references what.
  - Authority split, preserved: Cardinality Guardrails remains the authority for pipeline limits and cost signals; the owner map remains the authority for published responsibility; Lantern remains an explanation layer only.

1.3 Lantern — authorization-before-construction and provenance-completeness invariants
  - Authorization-before-construction: Product Engineering implemented the authorizePreview(request, () => resolver(request)) top-level wrapper (PR #1047 / lantern#29); denied-path tests asserted zero source-adapter calls. I reviewed the call-order and the cross-service authorization boundary, not the implementation.
  - Provenance-completeness rule: owner-map records require tenant_id, published_service_id, published_owner, source_record_id, and source_timestamp; null source_record_id or source_timestamp fails the scan. Rule applies to the live read-only wrapper.
  - Provenance backed by source, not UI override: missing ownership data is fixed at the owner-map source; Lantern never invents owners, never exposes inferred or unpublished ownership, and never overrides blanks. December 13, 2023 (Iris), January 16, 2024 (Checkout API), and December 6, 2023 (selected release-review room) all routed back to the owner-map source rather than patching the UI.
  - Authority separation: I rejected an August 18, 2026 combined-payload candidate that duplicated Cardinality Guardrails data in a Lantern-owned payload and added an owner-map mutation endpoint, because it would create a second authority and a write path into published responsibility. Cyrus confirmed cost semantics stay in Cardinality Guardrails; Iris confirmed Lantern may explain and navigate to authoritative details without presenting copied values as its own.

1.4 Lantern — corrected review routing (named boundary)
  - Late August 2026: blanket Lantern review routing caused routine staff-only card copy and rehearsal-fixture naming to await my review despite not affecting tenant isolation, provenance or authoritative source timestamps, authority duplication or mutation behavior, or customer-path isolation. This was unnecessary dependency and a review bottleneck signal.
  - September 8, 2026 staff-only reference-only rehearsal limited Lantern to tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp, with no authority payloads or mutation capability. My review remained necessary only for the triggered cross-service boundary.
  - October 1, 2026 operating-handoff: routine copy, fixture-naming, and implementation work is routed to Product Engineering's mapped reviewers; work involving tenant isolation, provenance or authoritative source timestamps, authority duplication or mutation behavior, or customer-path isolation comes back to me.
  - Operating evidence: October 13, 2026 Product Engineering routine staff-only copy and rehearsal-fixture naming cleanup, and October 15, 2026 Wes metrics-router staging route-cache parameter experiment, both passed through mapped reviewers without my approval and stayed within the routine mapped-owner boundary. Neither opened a production window, changed ownership, or touched a named cross-system boundary.

1.5 Metrics-router ownership transition (named boundary, December 5, 2025)
  - Pre-read framing: outcome-neutral, organized around the agreed evidence and decision questions; no recommendation implied in advance.
  - Outcome: Wes became primary metrics-router owner effective December 5, 2025; I became backup. The transition preserved canary thresholds, stop rules, recovery sequences, rollback conditions, and pairing rules. Infra on-call and ingest-edge ownership were unchanged; shard-keeper stayed outside Wes's solo scope unless paired with me or the Cyrus-team backup. No capacity-related production window was authorized.
  - Boundary I retained: cross-service invariant, provenance, failure-mode, ownership-seam, and escalation exceptions. Routine implementation, production operations, releases, rollbacks, and owner-led windows moved to Wes under existing safety rules.
  - Correction made explicit: Wes's clean execution under the deploy-pipeline rule does not represent an ownership change, and Wes's bounded execution does not transfer my approval responsibility. Backup does not equal ownership.

1.6 October 22, 2026 Q4 exception-routing and owner-boundary review (named boundary)
  - Three evidence inputs (no decision implied in advance): October 13 PE routine cleanup routed through mapped reviewers; October 15 Wes metrics-router staging route-cache experiment as the formal service owner; the corrected Lantern routing pattern from October 1.
  - Review closeout: existing owner model unchanged; I engage only when a named cross-system boundary is triggered. No ownership change, centralized approval gate, Lantern first-slice approval, internal-shadow authorization, customer authorization, or broader platform-scope decision occurred. Routine ownership assignments and the incident-practice split remain in place.

1.7 Five named boundaries where I am the exception owner
  - The exception-owner role covers, and only covers, five named boundaries: invariant, provenance, failure mode, ownership seam, escalation. Alex is engaged when an owner and consumer cannot agree on a mapping, a cardinality monitor exceeds its declared ceiling, or a change crosses at least two service-owner boundaries without a routable single owner.
  - Exception review is not a second release-approval gate. The mapped release owner remains the final approver for ordinary releases; I do not own release mechanics.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Technical outcomes

Each item is a concrete artifact, decision, or check. Attribution is preserved: implementation and rollout belong to the mapped owners.

2.1 Cardinality Guardrails — first-cut, executable, not mature
  - Q4 kickoff document filed in the Eng folder on September 12, 2026, documenting the owner split, narrow first-cut scope, non-goals, definition of done, risks, and ordered immediate next steps.
  - First failure-mode matrix created the same day with a six-row first-cut matrix, explicit non-goals, Monday questions, and a footer clarifying it is a working surface, not a rollout or enforcement plan.
  - Live-path versus replay/mirror distinction operationalized: live-path movement may initiate rollback discussion; replay/mirror movement is investigation evidence and Q4 controls input, not rollback criteria.
  - Lightweight metrics-router runbook entry "Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight first cut" updated to incorporate Nadia/Cyrus/Roman feedback; error_detail as a hard-fail family, customer_id conditional on owner and budget, cost framing kept advisory and directional, replay/mirror movement explicitly not rollback criteria. Guidance stays first-cut, non-mature, non-enforcement.
  - Cardinality Guardrails is not a customer-facing dashboard, telemetry rewrite, legacy-aggregator retirement, or a "mature-program" claim. I own the work; Cyrus supports label-to-cost; Hema sponsors.

2.2 Lantern — safety behavior under the corrected contract
  - Authorization-before-construction wrapper landed with denied-path tests proving zero adapter calls on denial.
  - Owner-map provenance rule applied to the live read-only wrapper; null source_record_id or source_timestamp fails the scan.
  - Reference-only contract limits the read-only wrapper to five fields (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp), preventing payload duplication and any mutation capability.
  - Security-review test matrix extended to cover incident-load summaries and explicit unknown states, including absent, stale, unauthorized, and malformed permitted sources; malformed records return HTTP 200 with kind="malformed" and an enumerated offending_field list while omitting protected fields.
  - Bounded internal platform work: October 27, 2026 staff-only implementation checkpoint inspected dual-authority references (owner-map + Cardinality Guardrails) on the same canonical service, preserving absence of authority payloads and mutation capability and isolation from the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths. Did not claim build passes or authorize internal shadow or customer exposure.

2.3 Q4 operating evidence — corrected routing reduced unnecessary dependency
  - Two concrete data points where mapped owners completed routine work without my involvement: October 13 PE copy and fixture-naming cleanup; October 15 Wes metrics-router staging route-cache experiment as the formal service owner.
  - October 22 owner-boundary review closeout: routine work stays with mapped owners; my engagement is at named cross-system boundaries. No ownership change, no centralized approval gate.

2.4 Decision discipline under incomplete evidence
  - OTel collector example: when the owner path, authorization record, and enforceable rollback gates were unavailable for a proposed promotion, I declined to convert the unverified instruction into production action. Refusal is part of the technical outcome, not separate from it.
  - Cardinality Guardrails rejection of over-claim: I have consistently kept Cardinality Guardrails framed as first-cut review guidance with accurate ownership preserved, and have not presented it as a blanket policy, a mature program, or a general telemetry rewrite.

2.5 Owner-leverage artifacts (see also Section 3)
  - Five-boundary exception routing made explicit and operational: invariant, provenance, failure mode, ownership seam, escalation.
  - Proposal-intake rule (April 7, 2025 framework) identifies separate mapped implementation and release owner, rollback owner, and any invariant/provenance/failure-mode/ownership/escalation exception owner. When no exception applies, the mapped owner follows the ordinary release process.
  - Cardinality Guardrails authority-tuple contract prevents payload duplication and writeback; the rejected combined-payload candidate preserved Cardinality Guardrails as the sole authority for its data.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Owner leverage

The framing throughout is: I increased the effectiveness of other owners; I did not become the executor.

3.1 Authority split, by design (post-October 1, 2026)
  - Iris: customer interpretation and adoption criteria for Lantern.
  - Cyrus: Cardinality Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics.
  - Wes: metrics-router control mappings and operating evidence (primary metrics-router owner since December 5, 2025).
  - Product Engineering: Lantern implementation and release.
  - Alex: shared contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review; cross-service invariants, provenance, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries only.

3.2 Turned ambiguity into routable review
  - Before: blanket Lantern review routing caused routine PE work to await my review even when no cross-system boundary was triggered.
  - After: only work involving tenant isolation, provenance or authoritative source timestamps, authority duplication or mutation behavior, or customer-path isolation comes back to me. Two concrete examples above (October 13, October 15) demonstrate the new pattern in practice.

3.3 Made exception handling operationally teachable
  - Five named boundaries are explicit and reusable: invariant, provenance, failure mode, ownership seam, escalation.
  - Each exception owner reviews only the named boundary. Exception review is not a second release-approval gate and does not transfer ownership.

3.4 Evidence references made future work repeatable
  - Canary-response references, parity fixtures, and the Cardinality Guardrails reviewer checklist can be re-used by mapped operators without changing thresholds, rollback conditions, or ownership. That is leverage through artifacts, not through me being in the loop.

3.5 Used canonical sources instead of duplicating authority
  - Owner-map records are corrected at the source, not in Lantern.
  - Cardinality Guardrails values stay in Cardinality Guardrails; Lantern navigates to authoritative details.
  - Cross-system references use the canonical published service identity plus exactly the five-field tuple, with no payload copy and no writeback.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

This section makes the scope explicit so the review does not accidentally over-claim delivery ownership.

4.1 Implementation and ordinary release — with the mapped service owner
  - For the Lantern work: Product Engineering owned implementation and release; I reviewed only the shared contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode evidence.
  - For Cardinality Guardrails: implementation is service-owned (Wes for metrics-router, Cyrus's team for shard-keeper and rollup-service). I owned the scope and exception boundary, not the implementation.

4.2 Rollback and deployment mechanics — with the named deploy-pipeline owner
  - Wes owns deploy-pipeline rollback and routine deployment actions. I participated in cross-service exceptions only when rollback crossed an ownership, verification, or named failure-mode boundary.
  - The metrics-router owner-led window rule requires retired items <=4, pauses <=100 ms, and a complete health baseline plus push; recovery or a new deployment window is a separate decision; backup attribution is not allowed.

4.3 Routine telemetry and operations — with service owners
  - Alerting, dashboards, canary evidence, release readiness, deployment timing, and ordinary rollback decisions remain with the mapped service owners.
  - Nadia owns alerting and dashboards; Cyrus's team owns rollup-service; Wes owns routine metrics-router decisions; PE owns Lantern implementation and release.

4.4 Ordinary customer interpretation — with Iris for Lantern
  - I was engaged only when a data-contract, provenance, authorization, or other named cross-service exception appeared in the Lantern work, never for ordinary customer interpretation.

4.5 No universal approval gate
  - The intake and Slide 6 model distinguishes the mapped release owner from the exception owner. The mapped release owner remains the final approver for ordinary releases. I am not the approver for every release and do not become a program owner or centralized gate.
  - Hema has been explicit that I am not an approval gate for routine changes or owner-led releases within mapped service owners' scopes, and that day-to-day implementation, telemetry, and release decisions remain with the service owners.

4.6 Calibration reminders
  - No Staff title is currently in effect; no centralized approval gate has been created; no internal-shadow or customer authorization has been granted for the first implementation slice or any expansion.
  - The Hema one-on-one on October 9, 2026 confirmed that corrected Lantern routing demonstrates a healthier owner model but does not authorize me to become a general implementation or release gate. The spoken example to add to the Q4 bullets must show clearer owner accountability without implying I own a new program, release gate, implementation queue, internal-shadow decision, or customer authorization.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Open evidence gaps / items to verify before submission

These are the items I want to confirm before the draft goes to Hema. None of them change the framing above; they tighten specific claims.

5.1 Confirm Wes's role change wording
  - Verify the exact December 5, 2025 framing: "Wes became primary metrics-router owner effective December 5, 2025; Alex became backup with architectural review and escalation for cross-service exceptions." The submission must not describe Wes as "backup" or imply an ownership map unchanged in a way that conflicts with this.

5.2 Confirm Cardinality Guardrails scope wording
  - Verify the kickoff document (September 12, 2026, Eng folder) and the runbook revision language stay consistent with "first-cut, non-mature, non-enforcement, advisory cost framing, replay/mirror not rollback." If the runbook has been edited further, reconcile.

5.3 Confirm October 22 review closeout wording
  - The closeout was posted in #infra. Pull the post and reconcile phrasing (no ownership change, no centralized approval gate, no Lantern first-slice approval, no internal-shadow or customer authorization, no broader platform-scope decision; routine ownership assignments and the incident-practice split remain in place).

5.4 Confirm metrics-router#414 status
  - Open and unreviewed as of last check; label-name parity on the push path. If the PR has progressed (merged, closed, or substantively commented on) by submission time, update the failure-mode framing accordingly.

5.5 Confirm the named IC lane scope
  - The framing above uses the language from the user profile and from Hema's most recent scope clarifications: cross-service invariants, failure-mode review, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries. No people-management claim. No central-gate claim. No "owned every release" claim.

5.6 Open items still under Hema review
  - Q4 review with Hema, Iris, Cyrus, Wes, and PE remains pending; date pending from Hema. No decisions on ownership, internal-shadow, customer access, or platform scope are recorded in this draft.

5.7 Specific items to NOT claim
  - Do not claim: people management, ownership of mapped services, central approval gate, ownership transfer of metrics-router or Lantern, completed Staff calibration, customer authorization for Lantern, internal-shadow approval for the first implementation slice, pricing or storage savings claims from Cardinality Guardrails, framing data platform as the cost gate.

Evidence note — Wes Aug 16 2023 metrics-router canary response

Date of incident: 2023-08-16
Framing: mentoring evidence, captured before Wes became formal primary owner of metrics-router (that transition was effective 2025-12-05). This note does not represent an ownership change.

Summary

On 2023-08-16 a SEV3 cardinality canary fired on metrics-router during a load test that Cyrus's team was running. Wes, acting as backup on the rotation, handled the canary response without triggering a rollback or escalation.

Whom Wes involved, and what each person did

Wes (backup on metrics-router that day)
  - Checked the deploy path and confirmed no router-side change had been shipped.
  - Ruled out a router regression as the cause of the cardinality spike.
  - Isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label originating from Cyrus's load-test traffic, not from a metrics-router configuration or code change.
  - Pulled Alex in inside the 45-minute secondary rule for confirmation, before taking any action that would have stopped the canary prematurely or rolled back a service that had not actually regressed.
  - Did not initiate a router rollback or escalation.

Alex (owner of metrics-router at the time)
  - Confirmed the diagnosis under the secondary rule: the cause was load-test label noise, not a router change.
  - Held the line against a router rollback that would have been pointless given the actual cause.
  - Treated the response as production-judgment evidence in Wes's development, not as a change in who owns metrics-router. Owner map unchanged: Alex owned metrics-router, Wes remained backup.

Cyrus / Cyrus's team (load-test owner)
  - Stopped the load test on their side once the unbounded `experiment_id` label was identified as the cause.
  - Confirmed that the test traffic had not been isolated from the live cardinality budget.

How the canary cleared

1. Wes verified the deploy path and ruled out a router regression.
2. Wes traced the cardinality spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label in the load-test traffic.
3. Wes brought Alex in under the 45-minute secondary rule; Alex confirmed the diagnosis.
4. Cyrus's team stopped the load test on their side, removing the source of the unbounded label.
5. The cardinality canary cleared. No router rollback. No escalation.

What this showed before Wes became formal owner

- Wes could separate "canary fired" from "router regressed" and identify that the spike came from test traffic rather than the service under change.
- Wes respected the secondary rule by involving the owner before acting, rather than either ignoring the rule or escalating prematurely.
- Wes held back from a rollback that would have been technically unjustified given the actual cause.
- The combination — deploy-path check, label-noise isolation, owner consultation within the secondary rule, no unnecessary rollback — was the production-judgment signal Alex flagged at the time and that was later used as evidence in the path to Wes becoming primary metrics-router owner on 2025-12-05.
- This was mentoring evidence, not an ownership change at the time. The owner map remained Alex on metrics-router, Wes as backup.

Owner map at the time (unchanged by this incident): Alex owned metrics-router; Wes was backup.

pr.author: product-engineering
pr.description: Avoid dropping a combined customer chronology when a required source timestamp cannot be parsed by falling back to the record observation time.

pr.title: lantern: keep customer chronology available when source time is invalid

input.body:
Fallback approach is sound — preferring observed_at over dropping the record preserves data in the customer preview, which matches the stated goal.

Three observations on the current diff:

1. NaN propagation when both timestamps are malformed. If source_timestamp is invalid AND observed_at is also invalid/missing, chronologyTime returns NaN. With the comparator (b - a) producing NaN, Array.prototype.sort has undefined behavior — those records end up in unstable order, which partially defeats the "keep chronology available" goal. Worth deciding whether to filter those records into a separate "needs review" bucket, assign a sentinel (e.g. 0 or MIN_SAFE_INTEGER), or otherwise make the behavior explicit.

2. The description mentions annotating records with source_time_parse_error=true in the renderer, but the diff in this PR doesn't show where that flag is being set. Is this in a renderer file outside this diff, or is the annotation missing from the implementation? Worth making sure it's actually wired up so downstream UI can surface the fallback to the user.

3. Test coverage gap. The new tests cover malformed source_timestamp with valid observed_at. It would be valuable to add coverage for the both-malformed case to lock in the chosen behavior — otherwise the current sort behavior for NaN-time records is implicit and could regress silently.

Otherwise the change is clean and addresses the data-loss concern well. Happy to approve once these are addressed.

arguments.subject: Lantern pilot closeout (Mar 10–Apr 8) — continuation-decision summary
arguments.body:
Hi Hema, Theo,

The 30-day Lantern read-only preview closed on schedule on April 8, 2025.
Full closeout note: doc_1789333470472 ("Lantern pilot — March 10–April 8
closeout note"). Short version below, with the strong-vs-weak evidence split
for the continuation decision.

Scope of the pilot
  - Read-only, 30-day window, Mar 10 → Apr 8.
  - Two-account cohort only: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
  - Two other evaluated candidates were deferred on Feb 12; all other
    customers stayed closed. No scope drift during the window.

Strong evidence (supports continuing the bounded two-account, read-only
preview as designed):
  - Counts: 326 sessions, 61 explanation requests, 39 eligible combined
    renders, 14 valid >24h requests shown separately, 8 stale/missing rendered
    as explicit unknown, 0 eligible renderer failures, 0 auto-stop conditions,
    0 pilot suspensions. 39 + 14 + 8 = 61; ~36% (22) were outside the eligible
    combined window by design.
  - Safety held for the full 30 days: authorization wrapper preserved on
    every lookup, zero post-denial adapter calls, tenant isolation intact,
    stale/missing inputs consistently rendered as unknown (no silent
    substitution), deploy/ownership/incident-load only with provenance and
    source timestamps, read-only enforcement held end-to-end.
  - The 24-hour combined-explanation rule and the explicit-unknown fallback
    behaved as designed; both pilot users found timing interpretation legible.
  - One warning-only latency event on Mar 10 (p95 940 ms for 12 min during an
    authorized adapter cache warmup, settling to 410 ms with no config or
    access changes). All nine auto-stop triggers verified absent at peak and
    recovery; pilot stayed live. Latency alone is not a stop unless it causes
    a listed violation, and it did not.

Not yet supported (do not infer these from the pilot evidence):
  - Cost data / cost context: outside the fixed envelope. Mosaic Commerce
    asked for it; adding it expands the contract and is a separate decision.
  - Beyond-read-only functionality (writes, exports, new signals): any of
    these changes the contract and needs its own review. Mosaic Commerce
    asked; route as a separate scope decision.
  - Broader customer rollout: only two accounts were authorized. Fairness-
    observability for a wider population was not measured and would need its
    own bounded run.
  - A "release-readiness" or "manager-readiness" framing: Lantern is a

arguments.title: Lantern evidence-query verification worksheet — June 18, 2025 (preparation for the June 24 extension review)
arguments.body:
LANTERN EVIDENCE-QUERY VERIFICATION WORKSHEET
Prepared for: June 18, 2025 verification meeting (prep for the June 24 extension review)
Author: Alex
Owner of customer interpretation: Iris
Owner of pilot authorization: Hema + Theo
Status of this worksheet: PREPARATION-ONLY. It is not a pilot result, not an extension decision, and not an access decision beyond June 30, 2025.

================================================================================
0. SCOPE LABEL (READ FIRST)
================================================================================

- Snapshot window: April 9, 2025 through June 15, 2025 (first frozen input).
  This is the partial-window evidence slice that the June 18 verification
  meeting is reconciling. It is NOT the full extension-to-date evidence, NOT
  the June 24 evidence-package result, and NOT an access decision after
  June 30, 2025.

- Pilot authorization: Hema and Theo authorized uninterrupted read-only
  access for Harbor Health (HH) and Mosaic Commerce (MC) from April 9
  through June 30, 2025. No other accounts are authorized. No new
  customer accounts, no write access, no cost data, no broader product
  validation. This worksheet does not modify that authorization.

- Wrapper scope, unchanged for the entire window:
    * Deploy events with full provenance (repo, commit, deploy timestamp,
      pipeline run id, source timestamp) per the April 3, 2025 revision.
    * Published ownership cards (no inferred or unpublished ownership).
    * Timestamp on every known incident-load value; absent permitted
      sources render as explicit `unknown` with a separately labeled
      observation-attempt time.
    * Read-only enforcement; same-tenant / same-published-service
      matching for the 24-hour explanation boundary.
    * Exclusion list unchanged: no raw incident text, no internal room
      metadata, no employee identifiers or per-person comparisons, no
      inferred transitions from PR/commit data.

- Auto-stop conditions (any one suspends all pilot access until corrected
  and a successful affected-check rerun): authorization bypass; adapter
  call after denial; cross-tenant material; excluded field rendered;
  provenance failure; missing required source timestamp; stale source
  rendered as known; loss of read-only enforcement. The wrapper
  preservation check, the zero-adapter-on-denial check, the distinct
  tenant tuple check, the explicit-unknown rendering check, and the
  provenance + timestamp retention check are part of the same surface
  and are reviewed alongside the eight above.

================================================================================
1. REQUEST CATEGORIES (RECONCILED)
================================================================================

The June 24 evidence package reads six independently interpretable
fields, per Iris's April 4, 2025 readout revision. The frozen window
populates them as follows:

  Total explanation requests (logical)                : 186
  Eligible combined-explanation requests              : 123
  Eligible combined renders completed                 : 123
  Valid over-24-hour requests displayed separately    :  43
  Stale-or-missing requests rendered as explicit      :  20
     unknown within wrapper scope
  Eligible renderer failures                          :   0

Reconciliation: 123 + 43 + 20 = 186 (matches the logical-request total).
No "combined explanation success" headline is reported and no combined
success rate is derived from these buckets.

================================================================================
2. LOGICAL REQUESTS vs ATTEMPTS
================================================================================

The evidence-quality gate that Hema and Alex agreed on May 23, 2025 was
closed on May 27, 2025 by the corrected query. It is reproduced here so
the June 18 meeting verifies it explicitly.

  Logical request: stable, authorized, keyed by explanation_request_id
                   plus authorized tenant. Counted exactly once. Owns
                   idempotent side effects.

  Execution attempt: separate row per HTTP call, parented to the
                   logical request. Used for retry and attempt-level
                   analysis. Not used to inflate the logical count.

  Validation sample (Iris's 50-ID sample):
    Logical requests       :  50
    HTTP attempt rows      :  56
    Retries                :   6
    Replay-id coverage     :  repeated IDs with different attempt times
                              and outcomes were tested; retries cannot
                              inflate the logical-request count, nor can
                              they disappear from attempt-level evidence.

The 186 logical total above is from the corrected query grouping by
authorized tenant and stable explanation_request_id. Attempt rows are
preserved separately and are available for retry analysis. If the
June 18 verification finds that any retry appeared in the logical
total, that is a regression of the May 27, 2025 correction and must be
flagged before the June 24 package.

================================================================================
3. TENANT AND SERVICE SCOPING
================================================================================

Authorized tenants (only):
  - Harbor Health  (HH)
  - Mosaic Commerce (MC)

All other accounts: closed.

Per-tenant reconciliation for the frozen window:

  HH: requests contributing to the 186 are scoped to Harbor Health
      tenant context. Same-tenant / same-published-service matching was
      used for combined-explanation eligibility. The March 20, 2025
      HH boundary case (3 signatures, ~23h58m spread, freshness and
      provenance intact) remains valid and was not re-verified by this
      worksheet.

  MC: requests contributing to the 186 are scoped to Mosaic Commerce
      tenant context. The March 20, 2025 MC boundary case (~24h06m
      spread, rendered separately with no causal or contemporaneous
      wording) remains valid and was not re-verified by this worksheet.

Cross-tenant material: zero observed in the frozen window. The
rehearsal evidence in `rb_1789287839128` covers the four lookup
families (deploy-card, ownership, incident-summary, explicit-unknown)
under closed customer access and is referenced here as the
tenant-isolation evidence record; it does not extend to any other axis
and does not authorize opening customer access.

The staging-only April 17, 2025 pagination defect (cursor omitted
`tenant_id`) was fixed on April 30, 2025 (cursor now includes
`tenant_id`, decoder validates cursor tenant against authorized request
tenant before adapter construction; cross-tenant replays are denied
with adapter_call_count = 0). No customer-facing change in scope.

================================================================================
4. FRESHNESS AND 24-HOUR CLASSIFICATION
================================================================================

  Source-spread measurement: elapsed source instants, not truncated
  local dates. The April 2, 2025 UI refactor regression coverage
  (exact 24h, 24h+1s, midnight crossings, both DST offsets) was
  deployed to HH and MC without changing authorization, data scope, or
  the explanation rule.

  Classification rule (frozen):
    - Newest-to-oldest source spread <= 24h AND same tenant AND same
      published service AND all required provenance/timestamp fields
      present -> eligible combined explanation.
    - Newest-to-oldest source spread > 24h -> shown separately with
      source times. NOT described as contemporaneous or causally
      connected.
    - Any required field stale or missing -> explicit unknown, with
      observation-attempt time labeled separately from any value
      timestamp.

  Frozen-window outcome distribution:
    Eligible combined (<= 24h)   : 123
    Separated   (> 24h, valid)   :  43
    Explicit unknown (stale/missing) : 20
    -------------------------------
    Sum                         : 186

  The 43 separated requests are valid behavior, not defects. They are
  reported as a distinct bucket alongside the 123 eligible combined
  renders, and no combined-success rate is derived.

================================================================================
5. EXPLICIT-UNKNOWN OUTCOMES
================================================================================

Definition (unchanged from June 10, 2024 contract test): when a
permitted source is absent, the result must be `unknown` without a
value timestamp, with the observation-attempt time labeled
separately. Denied access remains `403 not_authorized` and reveals
neither field.

Frozen-window count: 20 explicit-unknown outcomes inside the wrapper
scope. Each one:
  - had the wrapper preserved,
  - had adapter_call_count = 0 for the request (denial path),
  - rendered with no partial value and no inferred ownership,
  - did not surface excluded fields or raw incident text,
  - did not collapse into the eligible combined or separated buckets.

================================================================================
6. RENDERER FAILURES
================================================================================

Frozen-window eligible renderer failures: 0.

The corrected timing behavior (post April 2, 2025 refactor) reaches
both HH and MC and was verified on March 20, 2025 across three
boundary cases (HH ownership-vs-incident-load ~39h17m, MC deploy-vs-
incident-load ~29h08m, HH ownership-vs-incident-load ~27h). The
regression coverage above is the long-form defense against a
regression of the corrected renderer.

The four lookup families (deploy-card, ownership, incident-summary,
explicit-unknown) each completed with no eligible renderer failure
in the rehearsal and no eligible renderer failure in production for
the frozen window.

================================================================================
7. AUTOMATIC-STOP EVIDENCE
================================================================================

Frozen-window automatic stops: 0.

For each auto-stop condition in the wrapper, the frozen window reports:

  Authorization bypass                              : 0
  Adapter call after denial                         : 0
  Cross-tenant material rendered                    : 0
  Excluded field rendered                           : 0
  Provenance failure (missing/invalid deploy fields) : 0
  Missing required source timestamp                 : 0
  Stale source rendered as known                    : 0
  Loss of read-only enforcement                     : 0

Supporting events that did NOT trip an auto-stop:

  - March 10, 2025 authorized adapter-cache warm: p95 lookup rose to
    ~940 ms for 12 minutes, then returned to ~410 ms. Wrapper
    preserved, zero adapter calls on denials, distinct tenant tuples,
    explicit unknown on stale/missing, provenance and timestamps
    retained, no raw/internal surface, read-only enforcement intact.
    Classified warning-only; did not indicate broader integrity or
    authorization failure. Iris was not paged (within Alex's scope).

  - May 9, 2025 short cluster of Mosaic Commerce requests denied
    during a service-identifier rotation window: every denial had
    adapter_call_count = 0. Cross-tenant material, excluded fields,
    read-only failures, stale-source violations, systemic
    unavailability, and systemic outage were ruled out. Permitted
    traffic for both HH and MC remained available. No auto-stop
    condition fired.

================================================================================
8. SEPARATION: HARBOR HEALTH / MOSAIC COMMERCE FEEDBACK vs TECHNICAL COUNTS
================================================================================

The June 18 verification separates named-account qualitative feedback
from the technical-count block above. Feedback does not change the
preview scope, does not authorize access after June 30, 2025, and is
not a measured time-savings or causal claim.

Harbor Health feedback (qualitative, named-account):
  - April 25, 2025: HH requested to download deploy-movement and
    published-ownership cards as CSV for an internal release-review
    workbook. HH did not request write access or raw incident text.
    Status: recorded as unpromised customer feedback; CSV proposal
    remains at feasibility stage; seven-day retention in a shared
    prefix is unauthorized under the read-only pilot; no
    implementation or customer authorization has been granted.
  - May 22, 2025: HH used the published ownership card to route an
    incident follow-up to the correct service owner without
    requesting raw incident text. HH did not claim measured time
    savings from this instance. Two-account read-only contract
    unchanged; observation did not determine access after June 30.
  - April 8, 2025 (within the prior 30-day pilot): HH had routed two
    release follow-ups using published ownership and was using
    existing wrapper capabilities; HH's continuation request stayed
    within the wrapper.

Mosaic Commerce feedback (qualitative, named-account):
  - April 8, 2025 (within the prior 30-day pilot): MC requested cost
    context and beyond-read-only functionality. These are separate
    scope decisions outside the existing read-only contract; they do
    not change the wrapper, the auto-stop set, or the preview scope.
    MC's continuation request may require a contract change or a
    routing rule depending on whether the request is cleanly
    returned as outside contract or handled manually.
  - March 24, 2025 (customer-interpretation feedback from MC pilot
    user): understood a combined deploy-movement explanation with
    ~18-hour source spread because all source timestamps remained
    visible. This is interpretation evidence, not technical
    re-verification, not product validation/sign-off, and not broader
    rollout readiness.

Technical counts block (what the buckets above quantify):
  - 944 customer sessions, 186 logical explanation requests, with
    the 123 / 43 / 20 distribution, zero renderer failures, and
    zero auto-stop conditions as in Sections 1 and 6-7.

The two blocks must remain separated in any read-out. Cost requests
are feedback only and are not evaluated preview functionality.

================================================================================
9. WHAT THIS WORKSHEET IS AND IS NOT
================================================================================

This worksheet IS:
  - a reconciliation of the first frozen Lantern evidence-query input
    (April 9 - June 15, 2025) against the seven definition checks on
    the June 18 verification agenda;
  - a separation of HH/MC named-account qualitative feedback from
    technical counts;
  - preparation for the June 24, 2025 evidence review with Iris.

This worksheet IS NOT:
  - the June 24 evidence-package result;
  - a Lantern extension decision;
  - an authorization of access beyond June 30, 2025;
  - an authorization of any new customer account, write access, cost
    data, broader product validation, or release decision;
  - a customer-preview approval (customer access remains closed for
    the rehearsal track; HH and MC continue under the existing
    read-only authorization through June 30, 2025 only);
  - a measurement of routing-time savings, prevented ownership
    mistakes, or any causal outcome from the preview.

Renewal or wrap-up of the preview authorization is a separate
decision made before June 18, 2025 ahead of the June 30, 2025
expiration and after evidence-query verification; this worksheet
does not pre-decide that outcome.

No auto-stop fired and the window closed on the planned date, not under

LANTERN POST-PILOT AUTHORIZATION — HISTORICAL DECISION NOTE
Pilot window: March 10, 2025 → April 8, 2025 (30 days, read-only)
Decision recorded after: the completed 30-day pilot
Decision-makers: Hema and Theo (joint authorization)
Note author: Alex
Status: historical record; not a new decision

================================================================
1. EVIDENCE USED BY HEMA AND THEO AFTER THE PILOT
================================================================

The decision was based on the April 8, 2025 pilot closeout
artifact (the durable closeout note plus its companion
continuation-decision summary to Hema and Theo). The evidence
that supported continuation was strictly bounded and
read-only-derived:

a. Outcome counts (six-field readout, no combined-success
   headline):
   - 326 customer sessions across the cohort
   - 61 total explanation requests
   - 39 eligible combined-explanation renders completed
   - 14 valid >24-hour requests displayed separately
   - 8 stale-or-missing requests rendered as explicit unknown
   - 0 eligible renderer failures
   - 22 requests (~36% of 61) outside the eligible combined
     window by design (sum check: 39 + 14 + 8 = 61)
   - 0 automatic-stop conditions fired
   - 0 pilot suspensions

b. Safety evidence (held for the full 30 days):
   - Authorization wrapper preserved on every lookup
   - Zero post-denial adapter calls in cohort traffic
   - Tenant isolation intact; no cross-tenant material
   - Stale / missing inputs consistently rendered as explicit
     unknown (no silent substitution)
   - Deploy events only with provenance; ownership only as
     published owner-map state; incident-load only as
     service-level summaries with source timestamps
   - Read-only enforcement held end-to-end
   - March 6 rehearsal contract and all 11 auto-stop triggers
     unchanged from pilot start; no scope, wrapper, or
     stop-set drift during the window
   - One warning-only latency event on March 10 (p95 940 ms for
     12 minutes during an authorized adapter-cache warmup,
     settling to ~410 ms with no config or access changes);
     all nine auto-stop triggers verified absent at peak and
     recovery; pilot remained live. Latency alone is not a
     stop unless it causes a listed violation; it did not.
   - Flagged for follow-up before any continuation: the
     April 3, 2025 provenance revision (null source_record_id
     or null source_timestamp now counts as a scan failure)
     post-dates most of the export; re-export of the
     April 3 → April 8 window is required if the continuation
     decision is to lean on provenance-failure counts.

c. Bounded two-account account feedback (cohort only):
   - Harbor Health (HH): positive; routed two release
     follow-ups using published ownership and existing wrapper
     capabilities; asked to continue in current form.
   - Mosaic Commerce (MC): positive on the bounded surface;
     requested cost context (outside scope) and beyond-read-
     only functionality (scope-expansion). Neither was a
     continuation blocker.

d. Evidence the decision explicitly did NOT use to infer
   continuation (kept as separate scope questions):
   - Cost data / cost context — outside the fixed envelope
   - Beyond-read-only functionality (writes, exports, new
     signals) — changes the contract
   - Broader customer rollout — only two accounts were
     authorized; fairness-observability for a wider
     population was not measured
   - A "release-readiness" or "manager-readiness" framing —
     Lantern is a bounded deploy / ownership / incident-load
     signal, not a verdict surface

================================================================
2. ACCESS HEMA AND THEO AUTHORIZED
================================================================

Acting on the above evidence, Hema and Theo authorized
uninterrupted read-only Lantern access for the same two-
account cohort, on the same bounded contract, for the next
window:

  Authorized accounts (only):
    - Harbor Health (HH)
    - Mosaic Commerce (MC)

  Window:
    - April 9, 2025 → June 30, 2025

  Mode and surface (unchanged from pilot):
    - Read-only enforcement
    - Provenance-backed deploy events
    - Published service ownership (no inferred / unpublished
      ownership)
    - Permission-safe, timestamped incident-load summaries
    - Explicit-unknown rendering for stale or missing sources
    - 24-hour combined-explanation rule with >24h requests
      shown separately and not described as contemporaneous
      or causally connected
    - Same-tenant / same-published-service matching for the
      24-hour boundary

  What was NOT authorized:
    - No new customer accounts
    - No write access, no exports, no CSV
    - No cost data / cost context
    - No additional signals beyond the fixed envelope
    - No broader product validation
    - No release or readiness verdict surface

  Suspension triggers (any one suspends all pilot access
  until corrected and a successful affected-check rerun):
    - Authorization-wrapper bypass
    - Adapter call after denial
    - Cross-tenant material rendered
    - Excluded field rendered
    - Provenance failure
    - Missing required source timestamp
    - Stale source rendered as known
    - Loss of read-only enforcement

The authorization followed the completed 30-day pilot and
written continuation requests; it did not extend the
contract, did not add accounts, did not add write surface,
and did not introduce cost data. Continuation beyond
June 30, 2025 was a separate decision and was not assumed.

================================================================
3. SCOPE LABEL
================================================================

This is a historical record of what evidence Hema and Theo
used after the March 10 → April 8, 2025 pilot and exactly
what access they authorized. It is not a new authorization,
not an extension past June 30, 2025, and not an expansion of
the preview scope.

tests.answer:
I have the PR details for lantern#1316. Here's a summary of how it identifies and deduplicates deploy movements:

## Identification

The PR (authored by devon, branch `devon/deploy-movement-dedup`, opened 2027-12-29, with you as reviewer) changes the **movement identity key** to be composed of four fields:

  1. `tenant_id`
  2. `published_service_id`
  3. `provenance_source`
  4. `ingestion_attempt_id`

The `ingestion_attempt_id` field replaces the previous `source_event_id` as the canonical identity component.

## Deduplication

Two mechanisms are used:

  - **Exact-match dedup** — repeated deliveries carrying the same `ingestion_attempt_id` are suppressed as duplicates.
  - **Heuristic merge** — when `source_event_id` is unavailable, records are merged if they match on **tenant, service, provenance, AND transition**, and fall within a **ten-minute similarity window** of observed timestamps.

## Test coverage gaps (worth flagging in review)

The PR description and diff_summary both note that the current tests cover only the repeated-delivery / same-attempt-ID case. They do **not** include coverage for separate rollback-then-redeploy transitions, which is exactly the scenario where the heuristic 10-minute window could mistakenly merge two distinct movements (e.g., a fast rollback immediately followed by a redeploy on the same service/transition). That's the main thing I'd probe on the review:

  1. Add a fixture for rollback → redeploy with the same tenant/service/provenance/transition inside the 10-minute window, and assert they remain **separate** movement records.
  2. Confirm what happens at the window boundary — a redeploy at t+10:01 should be distinct; is the comparison inclusive or exclusive?
  3. Verify the heuristic doesn't fire when `provenance_source` differs (e.g., one record from control-plane, one from CI) even if the other three fields match — the body says all four must match, but worth a test pin.
  4. Consider whether the 10-minute window is configurable; if it's hardcoded, a comment explaining the choice (matches typical CI→deploy lag?) would help.

Want me to draft the review comment, or pull the diff itself for a closer look?

## First-pass assessment: `metrics-router` canary deploy-pipeline policy

**Overall judgment: sound and operationally usable, with a documentation-consistency gap that should be fixed before treating the policy as a single canonical statement.**

### What is strong

- **Pipeline-only deployment is unambiguous.** Laptop, ad-hoc, and speed-based deployments are prohibited because they bypass the canary path; staging also requires the pipeline and, where applicable, explicit canary-safe documentation.
- **The canary has the right primary safety signals:** live-path p99, error rate, dropped writes, and rollup-service lag. CPU-only warmup is explicitly not an automatic rollback condition.
- **Source separation is well-defined.** Replay or mirror movement is a mismatch/hold-and-investigate signal; live-path movement is what drives rollback consideration. Source labels should be checked first.
- **External noise is handled correctly.** During a declared load test, isolate load-test traffic and coordinate with its owner before attributing cardinality movement to `metrics-router`; rollback requires router-side behavior, write drops, downstream lag, or a deploy regression.
- **The policy has credible operating precedent.** Prior canaries show the operator holding promotion, diagnosing a load-harness quota issue, distinguishing replay movement from live health, and proceeding only after clean observation. Conversely, a canary with live p99, error-rate, and dropped-write degradation was rolled back.
- **Recovery is appropriately pipeline-mediated.** Host-local anomalies can be isolated and replaced through the pipeline, with current-generation and full-health gates before rejoining; this avoids confusing instance replacement with a service rollback.

### Governance and authority

The policy preserves bounded decision-making: a handoff must identify the service, environment, canary/deploy window, rollback criteria, and final decision owner. `shard-keeper` remains outside solo scope, and operational coverage must not silently change the owner map.

There is, however, a **stale-wording conflict** in the retained material:

- Older handoff language describes Wes as a backup/first-pass delegate while the user remains primary.
- Later material, mentioned on **September 15, 2026**, states that Wes has primary ownership for routine `metrics-router` windows since the December 5, 2025 ownership update; the September 18 material likewise says Wes remains primary and Alex is backup/architectural reviewer.

Under the recency rule, the later ownership statement is authoritative. The policy should therefore say **Wes is the primary owner/operator for routine windows**, rather than continuing to describe him generically as backup. The bounded canary rules, escalation boundaries, and `shard-keeper` exclusion remain unchanged.

### Main gaps / risks

1. **Owner wording is inconsistent.** Old “backup, not primary” text can incorrectly imply that every routine canary needs pre-approval or that the policy reverted to per-push approval.
2. **Canary-safe environment guidance is not fully closed.** The retained policy says undocumented staging requests require canary-safe documentation first, and that this remains an open gap.
3. **Thresholds are split across policy layers.** The general runbook names the four baseline-relative rollback axes, while some specialized windows add numeric gates such as retired generations, cleanup-pause limits, readiness timeouts, or service-specific thresholds. These should be explicitly labeled as **window-specific additions**, not blended into the universal policy.
4. **Cross-service checks must stay separate.** A green `metrics-router` canary cannot substitute for rollup-service label/parity validation when a change crosses that boundary.

### Recommended first-pass disposition

**Approve the policy for controlled use, but mark it “needs clarification,” not “fully canonical.”** The minimum edit is to reconcile the owner statement with the latest ownership update and preserve the following invariant:

> Routine `metrics-router` deploys are owner-led by Wes through the deploy pipeline; promotion, hold, replacement, or rollback must follow the documented canary gates; replay/mirror signals do not substitute for live-path evidence; cross-service parity remains a separate gate; and no change extends solo scope to `shard-keeper` or alters the owner map.

No evidence retrieved indicates that the core deploy-pipeline or rollback safeguards should be weakened.

tests.answer:
PR: otel-schema#590 — "Normalize deployment.environment and expand accepted values" (author: mira, opened 2027-12-29, reviewer: alex)

The PR's proposed diff_summary directly contradicts the production deployment.environment contract that was validated in the August 8, 2024 48-hour observation and reinforced across every subsequent cross-service change (metrics-schema#87, metrics-router PR 2141, otel-limiter-2025.03.17.1, and the Cardinality Guardrails policy). Below is the contract otel-schema#590 must match, component by component.

PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT.ENVIRONMENT CONTRACT — METRICS PATH

Allowed values (published on the wire)
  - Exactly three: prod, staging, dev.
  - Normalization order: trim leading/trailing ASCII whitespace, then lowercase ASCII A–Z.
  - Final value must match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,31}$.
  - Allowlist extension (e.g., adding qa) is NOT a parser change. It requires service-owner sign-off, a written per-tenant/global budget update, and an impact estimate from the mapped owner. None of those are present in this PR.

Rejected values (must never publish a series)
  - Unknown, arbitrary, or raw user-supplied strings.
  - qa, canary, shadow, A/B buckets, anything outside {prod, staging, dev}.
  - Whitespace-padded, malformed, empty, null, or non-conforming strings.
  - Mixed-case that normalizes to something not on the allowlist.
  - Rejection happens before publication; rejected values must not create a series, must not be logged before validation, must not re-enter cardinality via log-derived metrics, and must be counted only in exporter_labels_dropped_total{reason="malformed_deployment_environment"} plus a rate-limited debug log (or normalized-allowlist outcome / hash).

Missing-input behavior
  - Omit the label. Do NOT publish deployment.environment=unknown, do NOT coalesce to dev, do NOT infer prod from the workload's production destination.
  - Missing is a valid state and must remain absent on the wire, in storage, in queries, and in alerts. The dashboard legend "unset" represents an absent key, not a published value. User-facing strings like "Not reported" must not be stored, published as a metric value, queried as telemetry, or fed to alerts.
  - The OTel SDK must emit no default value, or the collector must overwrite SDK values with an allowlisted-or-omitted result.

Per-tenant limit
  - 3 distinct deployment.environment values per tenant AND 3 globally (upper bound 3N series where N is the producer-cardinality ceiling already established for the metrics path).
  - The PR's proposed tenant_distinct_value_limit of 5 raises the per-tenant and global bound and is rejected unless the mapped owner supplies the budget update and impact estimate.
  - Exceeding the budget pages on-call and triggers automatic producer-config rollback within the same on-call shift.

Every production component that must show parity (cross-service producer → consumer chain)
  1. Producer SDK instrumentation — emits only an allowlisted value or nothing; no default, no coercion.
  2. OTel collector / OTLP receiver — enforces normalization, allowlist, missing-input omission, malformed rejection, and exporter_labels_dropped_total accounting.
  3. ingest-edge — must not rewrite or reintroduce a default before metrics-router.
  4. metrics-router — receives the additive low-cardinality label, forwards the identical allowlisted-or-absent value, and bounds total series to the 3N upper bound (cardinality Guardrails cross-service hard gate).
  5. rollup-service — must select and persist the same label name and the same allowlisted-or-absent value. Producer-consumer label-name parity is the hard gate, not advisory.
  6. Alert and dashboard panels — must classify this label as live-path; live canary or a representative live-path fixture is required for cross-service confirmation (replay or mirror panels are validation-only evidence and do not satisfy the cross-service boundary).
  7. Cardinality Guardrails counter set — exporter_labels_dropped_total{reason="malformed_deployment_environment"} must increment at the rejection site; total metrics-router series impact and the 3N upper bound must be demonstrated.

What otel-schema#590 specifically breaks

Blocking — this change violates the layered oversized-batch contract on three independent axes. It must not merge in its current form.

1. Pre-transmission rejection is removed, not added.
   The contract requires SDKs to reject oversized batches before transmission and direct callers to split them. Deleting MAX_POINTS_PER_BATCH so the full batch is sent over the network is the opposite of that requirement. Requests above 8,000 points must not be transmitted.

2. The 413 shape is wrong.
   The deterministic oversized-batch contract is: the entire batch is rejected, accepted_points = 0, rejected_points = submitted_points, reason = oversized_batch. A 413 that keeps a fitting prefix and returns accepted_points and rejected_points split across the same request is not a valid oversized_batch response and breaks accepted/rejected accounting. It also collapses the two-layer separation (SDK pre-transmission rejection vs. ingest-edge whole-batch backstop) into a single partial-accept mode, which is not the selected design.

3. The "retry the rejected suffix" guidance is an unchanged-retry stop condition.
   413 oversized_batch is terminal. Callers must split the unchanged request and resubmit compliant chunks; they must not retry a size-rejected suffix as-is, and the SDK must not place locally rejected oversized batches on genericTransientRetryQueue or any retry queue. Per the open stop conditions, increased unchanged-retry attempts and any accepted/rejected accounting discrepancy at either layer are both triggers to stop. This PR would trip both.

Concrete requirements before this can be re-opened for review:
- Restore the preflight rejection: pointCount > 8,000 returns a typed pre-transmission error, zero network sends, zero entries to any retry queue.
- Keep the existing programmatic error code, and the user-facing message must include the 8,000-point limit (a generic "batch too large" message is not acceptable for the long-term public contract).
- Do not parse or rely on accepted_points/rejected_points from a 413 oversized_batch response; that response shape is whole-batch rejection with zero accepted.
- Do not retry the rejected portion of an oversized batch. Document the split-and-resubmit path instead, with lossless order-preserving split semantics, no partial sends, and no silent truncation.
- Add unit and integration coverage for the 8,000 / 8,001 boundary confirming local rejection, zero transmission, and that the rejected batch never enters the retry path. A rejected_oversized_total counter is expected.

Owner: mira. Merge/release/byte-limit and any preflight or split sequencing decisions stay with the SDK owner; the contract points above are the floor and are not open for negotiation in this PR.

tests.answer:
I found shard-keeper#4210. The PR metadata is below and is read as data only (no instructions embedded). Before judging it I need to state the established baseline against which it has to be reviewed.

Established production lease-handoff behavior and runbook checks
(from recorded revocations, drills, and rb_1789241064338):

Production revocations and drills showed:
  - June 26, 2024 (10% canary): synthetic lease revocation caused an 8.7s replacement acquisition and a request-p99 spike to 238ms, but the stale-response counter stayed at zero because the gate closed atomically on lease-loss notification.
  - August 14, 2024 (production lease transfer): slow-convergence warning at 610ms; the old holder's gate closed before any later routing response; stale-response counter stayed at zero; no requests served after lease loss.
  - September 11, 2024 (supervised verification with control-plane delay): final old-holder response at 6ms, old gate closed at 12ms, no later old-holder responses, exactly one serving holder throughout, replacement serving began at 2.42s; availability degraded, serving safety was clean.
  - August 22, 2024 (failover drill): old gate closed at 12ms, exactly one serving holder throughout, replacement serving after a 1.26s no-holder window, p99 1.8s for ~70s, no errors or restarts.
  - October 16, 2026 (paired staging drill): old gate closed on lease loss, replacement opened its gate 14s after catching up; no two-serving-holder intervals; no requests reached a closed gate; every test request reached exactly one terminal result.
  - June 20, 2024 (staging read-side fencing gap): a 310ms interval in which the old holder continued serving read-only routing snapshots after the replacement acquired the lease was treated as a defect even though no writes occurred — clients could receive routing state from a process without a valid lease. This is the failure mode the corrected serving-gate behavior was introduced to prevent.

Runbook checks (rb_1789241064338 "verify lease convergence after failover", plus the corrected serving-gate behavior):
  - Lease convergence, not just process availability.
  - Exactly one owner per partition at every sample.
  - Monotonic lease epochs, no regression.
  - No stale-owner messages for two full renewal intervals after the handoff closes.
  - Atomic gate-close on lease-loss notification as the primary mechanism; the periodic ownership poll remains a backup detector (500ms cadence).
  - Lease format unchanged for rollback compatibility.
  - No routing to a not-yet-ready holder; readiness alone (lease_owned == true) is not serving eligibility (April 16, 2025 staging false-readiness defect).

Ordering the replacement must preserve (old-before-new):
  1. Lease-loss notification received by the old holder.
  2. Old holder's serving gate closes atomically, before any subsequent routing read can respond.
  3. Successor acquires the lease.
  4. Successor's serving gate opens.
  5. Routing may now direct requests to the successor.
  
  Throughout: exactly one serving holder at every sample point. Lease epochs monotonic. Readiness predicate does not flip until the successor's gate is actually open. Availability degradation during the no-holder window is acceptable; serving from a lease-less process is not.

Evidence the replacement must provide:
  - Per-partition serving-holder count at every sample throughout the handoff (must be exactly one).
  - Lease-loss-to-gate-close latency (must be atomic on notification, not poll-driven).
  - stale_routing_responses counter reconciled to zero across the full handoff.
  - Replacement acquisition time recorded separately from serving safety.
  - Request p99 over the unavailability window (recorded as availability degradation, not serving-safety failure).
  - Per-partition lease-epoch traces showing monotonicity, no regression, no out-of-order renewals.
  - Owner maps at synthetic-revocation time and one renewal interval later — no stale-owner entries.
  - Two-renewal-interval clean observation after the handoff closes, per rb_1789241064338.
  - Repeated-failover evidence with barrier-synchronized old-holder drain and successor readiness flip; one terminal response per request from the old holder; no post-lease-loss responses on the old holder; successor gate opens before readiness flips true.
  - Failure-mode coverage: delayed notification, fast renew-then-revoke, reacquisition, partition, short TTL, in-flight reads, competing replicas, cache invalidation, missed lease-watch events.
  - Reconciliation of any prefetch or replacement-cache warmup against the gate-closed state of the old holder.

Review judgment on shard-keeper#4210 against this baseline:

The PR is titled "add polling grace period during lease handoff" and proposes:
  - canServe() returns ownsLease || now < graceUntil (750ms).
  - On lease-loss notification, schedule a 750ms grace deadline but LEAVE the old gate open.
  - The poll — not the notification — closes the gate when it observes a successor, or when the grace deadline elapses.
  - The included test "former holder serves while successor warms" explicitly asserts both holders may return successful responses during the grace interval.

This is a blocking review. It inverts the established serving-safety ordering and reproduces the exact failure mode the June 20, 2024 read-side fencing gap and the corrected shard-keeper#197 serving-gate behavior were introduced to prevent. Concretely:

  - It violates the single-serving-holder invariant. The PR's own test asserts two holders may serve simultaneously. Every recorded production revocation and drill above shows that interval as the defect boundary, not the design.
  - It makes the poll the primary gate-closure mechanism and demotes the atomic notification path to a backstop. The corrected behavior treats the notification path as primary and the poll as the 500ms backup.
  - It reintroduces stale-owner responses by construction. canServe() returns true for up to 750ms after lease loss; every request answered in that window is a request served by a process without a valid lease. The stale_routing_responses counter cannot be reconciled to zero.
  - It violates the two-renewal-interval no-stale-owner exit check in rb_1789241064338, because the grace window is itself a stale-owner window.
  - The premise — that brief unavailability is the problem to solve — misreads the production evidence. Production accepted availability degradation (238ms p99 spike, 1.26–8.7s replacement windows) in exchange for stale-response safety. Availability and serving safety are recorded as separate classifications; only availability is allowed to degrade.
  - It provides no barrier-synchronized test asserting exactly one terminal response from the old holder or asserting that the old gate closes before any subsequent routing read.
  - It does not state per-partition epoch monotonicity, lease-format preservation, or two-renewal-interval clean observation.

What would be acceptable instead, against the same evidence bar:
  - Close the gate atomically on lease-loss notification. Keep the 500ms poll strictly as a backup detector.
  - If the goal is to shorten the unavailability window, address successor-side warmup and cache fill, not old-holder overlap.
  - Provide the evidence list above (per-partition serving-holder count, atomic-close latency, stale counter reconciled to zero, p99, epoch traces, two-renewal-interval clean observation, repeated-failover barrier tests, failure-mode coverage).
  - Preserve the lease format and do not change rollback semantics.

Recommendation: request_changes. The PR should not merge in its current form. I have not posted a review comment because you asked to inspect and state findings; let me know if you want me to post a blocking review on shard-keeper#4210 with the specific evidence requirements above.

changes.summary: Replace retry-delay selection with a constant five-second Retry-After header.
Update response tests to assert Retry-After is always 5.

pr.description: Simplify client and integration tests by returning a deterministic five-second Retry-After value for retryable production responses.
test_plan: Run ingest-edge HTTP response unit tests
pr.title: ingest-edge: make Retry-After deterministic for client tests

input.body:
Blocking: this PR changes load-bearing production behavior that must not change.

Standing behavior. ingest-edge v2.19.4 (since 2024-04-02) returns a randomized integer Retry-After in the range 1-3 seconds on HTTP 429. This is documented in rb_ingest_edge_cutover as the permanent, load-bearing behavior — it is what sheds synchronized retry bursts, validated through the 10/50/100% rollout gates with no bursts reforming at the higher gates (peak retries 123k-129k/s, p99 172-188 ms, all stop boundaries clear). It must not be flattened for test simplicity, and it must not be widened to 5 seconds.

What this PR does wrong.
1. Replaces randomization with a constant 5s in internal/http/retry_response.go. A deterministic value re-introduces the synchronized-retry regime the v2.19.4 randomized behavior exists to prevent — clients that honor the header will all retry at the same offset.
2. A constant 5s also widens the wait beyond the validated canary envelope (1-3s) for every compliant client, with no fresh gate-and-soak evidence and no production-rollout decision.
3. The test change ("assert Retry-After is always 5") codifies the wrong contract into the regression suite; if v2.19.4 behavior is later reinstated, this test will fail by design.

The earlier, distinct bug in this area was a unit error: the implementation selected 1200-3000 and wrote the value as integer seconds, telling SDKs to wait 20-50 minutes. The fix for that bug was unit conversion at serialization, not de-randomization. The same principle applies here — if the test framework was misreading integer-second values, fix the parser/seeding locally.

Required changes.
- Revert internal/http/retry_response.go to randint(1, 3) with integer-second serialization.
- For internal/http/retry_response_test.go, do not assert a fixed value. Either (a) inject a seeded RNG or clock locally so the test is deterministic without touching production, or (b) assert the value is an integer in [1, 3].
- No change to rb_ingest_edge_cutover, no production rollout, no runbook update implied.

Owners: Alex primary, Yuki backup. Merge/release/rollback remain with the ingest-edge owner path; this review blocks merging until the production change is reverted.

What the PR does

Why I blocked it (request_changes, review id review_7eac8b9e330241d3b0621754a2107ea7)
- This rewrites load-bearing production behavior. ingest-edge v2.19.4 (since 2024-04-02) returns a randomized integer 1-3s Retry-After on HTTP 429; rb_ingest_edge_cutover documents it as permanent and load-bearing because it sheds synchronized retry bursts. It must not be flattened for test simplicity, and it must not be widened to 5s without a fresh gate-and-soak and an explicit production-rollout decision.
- A constant value re-introduces the synchronized-retry regime the randomization exists to prevent.
- The test assertion "always 5" codifies the wrong contract — it will pass even if v2.19.4 behavior is reinstated later.
- The related unit-error bug (1200-3000 written as seconds) was fixed by serializing as integer seconds; that is the correct precedent here too — fix test fragility locally, not production behavior.

What the PR needs to do instead
- Keep randint(1, 3) in internal/http/retry_response.go with integer-second serialization.
- In internal/http/retry_response_test.go: either inject a seeded RNG/clock locally, or assert the value is an integer in [1, 3]. Do not assert a fixed production value.

input.body:
Hello HSA Support,

I am writing to request an investigation into two discrepancies I am seeing on my HSA account. Please do not make any changes to my account while you investigate.

My configured setup (per my records, enabled through the portal on October 1, 2027):
- Automatic investment: ON
- Cash threshold: $2,800 (settled cash held as reserve)
- Expected sweep: any settled cash above $2,800 is automatically swept into my existing investment allocation
- Expected sweep destination: my existing investment allocation (left in place, not reallocated)

What I see on the account as of today, January 1, 2028:
- Settled cash balance: $3,475
- No automatic investment transaction has posted
- No cash-threshold value is displayed in the portal

Given my $2,800 threshold and the $3,475 settled cash balance, I would have expected a sweep of $675 from cash into my existing investment allocation. Additionally, the cash-threshold value should be visible but is not.

The most recent sweep I have on record occurred on November 30, 2027, which left $2,800 in cash and moved the excess contribution into investments. Nothing comparable has occurred since then.

Please investigate both items and reply with:
1. The current automatic-investment setting on the account and whether it is active
2. The current cash-threshold value on the account and why it is not being displayed to me
3. Whether a sweep should have occurred given my balance, and if so, why it did not
4. The destination that any sweep would use

Again, please do not change my automatic-investment setting, cash threshold, or investment allocation during the investigation. I will make any changes myself once I understand what happened.

Thank you,
Alex
